common_name: Golden Giant Amaranth (Tall Golden-Yellow Grain and Cut-Flower Amaranth)

planting.note: Sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Golden Giant bears tall, upright, golden-yellow seed plumes on a vigorous grain amaranth suited to both harvest and cut-flower use.

directions: Sow seeds shallowly, barely covered, in warm soil after the last frost, or start indoors a few weeks early. Golden Giant produces tall, dense, upright golden-yellow flower plumes on vigorous, sturdy stems, grown both for its abundant edible grain and as a dramatic fresh or dried cut flower for fall arrangements. Heat-tolerant and low-maintenance, it thrives in full sun and average soil, producing heavy yields of small, protein-rich seed by the time the plumes fully color and dry. Harvest seed heads once they rattle and the seed sheds easily when rubbed, then thresh and winnow; cut plumes for drying just as they color for the best cut-flower use, and expect self-sowing if seed heads are left in place.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

common_name: Cherry Vanilla Quinoa (Deep Cherry-Red and Cream Bicolor Quinoa)

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Cherry Vanilla quinoa prefers cool growing conditions and can bolt or perform poorly in extended hot, humid weather.

directions: Direct sow in early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun; quinoa performs best in cool weather and can struggle through extended hot, humid summers. Cherry Vanilla bears striking bicolor seed heads combining deep cherry-red and creamy vanilla-white tones on the same plant, one of the most visually dramatic quinoa selections available and prized as much for its ornamental cut-flower value as for its edible seed. The tall, colorful seed-head spikes make an eye-catching addition to a cutting garden as well as a productive grain crop. Harvest seed heads once they dry and the seeds rattle loosely, then thresh and winnow before rinsing to remove the bitter saponin coating and cooking or storing.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

common_name: Oro de Valle Quinoa (Southwestern Heirloom Golden Quinoa)

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Oro de Valle is a heat-adapted quinoa selection developed for the American Southwest, more tolerant of warm growing conditions than most quinoa varieties.

directions: Direct sow in early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun. Oro de Valle, meaning 'gold of the valley,' was developed in Arizona specifically to adapt quinoa to hot, arid, low-elevation growing conditions unlike the cool highland climate quinoa traditionally requires, making it one of the more heat-tolerant quinoa selections available for warmer American gardens. It produces bright golden seed heads on tall, upright stems, valued for both grain production and its striking garden presence. Harvest seed heads once they dry and the seeds rattle loosely, then thresh and winnow before rinsing to remove the bitter saponin coating and cooking or storing.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Sow after last frost; chia is a short-day plant that flowers in fall, so it is best suited to climates with a long frost-free autumn. Black Chia is the standard dark-seeded form most commonly grown and sold commercially.

directions: Surface-sow seed on a firm, moist seedbed and barely press in, as chia seed is mucilaginous and will stick to the surface when wet; thin plants to 18-24 inches once seedlings emerge. Black Chia is the standard, most widely grown dark-seeded chia strain, producing the small, deep-brown-to-black seeds most familiar from commercial chia products, on whorled flower spikes of small purple blooms that appear in autumn as day length shortens. Chia does not respond well to transplanting and should be direct-sown where it will grow. Harvest stalks when the calyces begin to dry and before birds consume the seed, placing harvested stalks head-first into paper bags to finish drying, then shake out seed and screen away debris.
